items.text: The block/event joint design in children's continuous natural speech can distinguish group differences related to fluent speech from activity related to specific stuttering events, going beyond resting-state and simple tasks.

The three groups—persistent, recovered, and non-stuttering—along with the continuous follow-up source, enable comparison of recovery-related patterns such as left-hemisphere normalization versus right-hemisphere compensatory processing, and provide hypotheses for subsequent longitudinal testing.

The radiation-free whole-brain continuous-speech sICA method, synchronized speech/behavior coding, and existing cohort can yield methodological feasibility and child effect estimates; inconsistency with adult predictions can also update understanding.

Reduced resting-state DVARS, consistency with adult PET, and a single-child demonstration do not sufficiently prove that neural signals are preserved and motion residuals eliminated during children's stuttering events; 9 mm is also not a universally reliable quality boundary.

Large adult effect size estimates do not fully align with 20 participants per group, numerous covariates, and imaging multiple comparisons; 300 syllables × 4.4% × 75% yields only about 10, and event exclusion will reduce 1b precision and select for highly symptomatic children.

Cross-sectional recovered-group differences cannot demonstrate recovery mechanisms or predict the future; treatment, development, and task language load can still explain the differences. The existing follow-up diagnosis improves group classification confidence but does not eliminate these explanations.
